definition: The pairing hypothesis is the idea that, in some temperate early-spring-breeding amphibians, mating pairs form most reliably through a two-stage process: some pairings begin before winter at or near breeding sites, and others occur again after emergence in spring. In the source, this is presented as the “surefire pairing hypothesis,” linking autumn female-first arrival, group hibernation, and spring male-first arrival to more secure pair formation.

reasons: The definition is not supported for the requested field of learning: the packet’s term is a hypothesis in amphibian reproductive behavior, not a psychology/learning concept.

It adds unsupported specifics such as “temperate early-spring-breeding amphibians,” “mating pairs form most reliably through a two-stage process,” and “autumn female-first arrival, group hibernation, and spring male-first arrival,” which are not stated as the definition’s general claim.

The packet uses the author’s proposed “surefire pairing hypothesis” in a specific biological context; the definition treats it as a broad established idea and recasts it in different wording without clear support.
